newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu rejects early elections.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu rejects early elections.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected opposition calls for early elections on Sunday despite the lingering fog of a corruption scandal.
In a further setback for the right-wing Likud party leader, an annual public opinion poll for the first time showed a majority of Israelis back a Palestinian state.
"I have no intention of going to early elections. I intend to correct what needs to be corrected and move forward," the prime minister, elected 11 months ago, told Israel Radio.
Israeli opposition politicians demand elections because of an influence-peddling scandal that has rocked his government.
The affair has overshadowed over efforts to put Middle East peacemaking, in deep crisis over Israeli settlement building in Arab East Jerusalem, back on track.

Opposition lawmaker Yossi Beilin, an architect of the landmark 1993 Oslo peace accords with the PLO, met Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat in the West Bank on Sunday and offered a formula for breaking the logjam in Middle East peacemaking.

Asked if the government would consider Beilin's initiative, which included an end to Jewish settlement building, Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan told Reuters: "No...Beilin cannot negotiate on behalf of the government."
A PLO official said Arafat accepted the initiative though Palestinians were pessimistic about its prospects.
"Nothing can be taken seriously unless it comes from the Israeli government," the official, who would not be named, said.
Arafat, asked by reporters if he might meet Netanyahu, said: "He is not willing to push forward the peace process."
Arafat's peace talks with Netanyahu have been frozen since the right-wing Israeli leader in March broke ground on a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem which triggered an outburst of violence.
Despite insufficient evidence to bring Netanyahu to trial, prosecutors said last week there were "real suspicions" about his role in the short-lived appointment of an attorney-general.
"There were certainly mistakes that I made -- I don't deny it -- throughout the whole selection process," Netanyahu told Israeli army radio.
Granting his first interviews to the Israeli media in the week since prosecutors decided not to charge him, Netanyahu said a new committee would prevent further mistakes.
Prosecutors say Shas party lawmaker Aryeh Deri should be charged in the scandal while the director-general of Netanyahu's office Avigdor Lieberman faces further investigation.
"The bottom line is I didn't break the law," Netanyahu said.

The annual poll by a leading think-tank found 51 percent of Israelis support the establishment of a Palestinian state while 49 percent oppose it. Netanyahu was narrowly elected prime minister last May on a platform steadfastly opposed to a Palestinian state.

"We have been conducting this poll for the last 10 years and this is the first time the figure has passed the 50 percent mark," said Professor Asher Arian of Tel Aviv University's Jaffee Centre for Strategic Studies.
The poll of 1,216 people with a 2.8 percent margin of error was done in February and early March before the peace crisis.

In the Gaza Strip, about 200 Palestinians demonstrated near a settlement on Sunday, charging Israel was expanding it. Arale Tzur, head of the Gaza council of Jewish settlements, said the Israeli army was only enlarging its position at the site.
In Palestinian-ruled Jericho, Arafat described as "a barbaric, shameful act" the stabbing to death of two Israeli women whose bodies were found in the West Bank on Friday.
He said Israeli and Palestinian officers met to discuss the issue. Israeli police said they were investigating whether the killers were Palestinian guerrillas.
